There is one more point to consider about al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī’s letter to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

As we have argued, ʿAbd al-Malik knew about al-Ḥasan’s fear of political authority.

passage-en-01354
That is why, we believe, he asked him for his opinion on free choice and compulsion. He expected al-Ḥasan to be too frightened to state his true position openly.

Perhaps, he thought, al-Ḥasan would give an obscure or ambiguous answer that could then be used as a weapon against the Qadarites.

But this time al-Ḥasan did not completely give way to fear.

passage-en-01357
His reply to ʿAbd al-Malik contains language which, in our view, did more than simply state the theoretical position of the Qadarites.

It also contained an indirect criticism of the Umayyad caliph.

passage-en-01359
This is the third point we wanted to make.

When al-Ḥasan wrote:

“Everything is by God’s decree and destiny except acts of disobedience,”

he was not simply stating an abstract theory.

We can also hear in these words an allusion to the sins committed by the Umayyad rulers.

And by “acts of disobedience,” we should not understand only their personal violations of religious or moral rules.

The term also includes social injustice, the shedding of Muslim blood and the seizure of Muslim wealth.

passage-en-01366
This is exactly what Maʿbad al-Juhanī and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār had in mind when they came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said:

passage-en-01367
“Abū Saʿīd, these kings shed Muslim blood and take Muslim wealth, and then they say, ‘Our actions happen only by the decree of God Most High.’”

Let us now return to Ibn al-Murtaḍā’s account of Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

passage-en-01369
We saw Ghaylān call on the righteous Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz to accept Qadarite doctrine.

passage-en-01370
We then saw the caliph summon Ghaylān and ask for his help in repairing the damage done by earlier Umayyad rulers, even though he himself disagreed with Ghaylān over the question of human freedom.

passage-en-01371
We also saw Ghaylān take charge of selling the treasures of the Umayyad rulers.

As he did so, he raised slogans with a clear social and class meaning.

Indeed, we can say that their content was directly concerned with class inequality.

While selling the Umayyad possessions in Damascus, he called out:

“Come to the possessions of the traitors! Come to the possessions of the oppressors!”

And again:

“What can I say to those who claim that these men were rightly guided leaders, when this is what they owned while people were dying of hunger?”

What can we conclude from this account?

The answer seems natural and logical.

We cannot separate the “theoretical principle” from the “practical position.”

Anyone following the logic of the evidence must see the real and direct connection between Ghaylān’s Qadarite doctrine and his position toward the Umayyads—between his ideas and his political conduct.

passage-en-01381
There is no split in Ghaylān’s personality here.

A split would exist only if his theory contradicted his actions, or if his principles contradicted his conduct.

passage-en-01383
But once we reject that contradiction, we can see that the two sides fit together completely.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01384
They are two sides of the same thing: one theoretical and one practical, one expressed as principle and one expressed through action.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01385
The same was true of Maʿbad al-Juhanī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01386
And it was also true of ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01387
All this leads us to a necessary conclusion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Qadarite doctrine took the particular theoretical form in which it appeared through the school of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī in Basra, then in Damascus, and then in Medina in the Hijaz, because it gave religious expression to an ideology growing on the opposite side of the struggle from the ideology of Umayyad rule: the doctrine of compulsion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01389
This conclusion does not mean that Qadarite doctrine had no connection with what has been called the philosophical needs of the human mind.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01390
Nor does it deny the importance of attempts to reconcile Qurʾānic passages.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01391
Nor does it deny the influence on Arab-Islamic thought of Christian theology, Persian religious thought or ancient Indian thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01392
Our point is simply that none of these factors was the fundamental cause of the rise of Qadarite doctrine.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01393
Different Western and Eastern scholars have taken one or more of these factors and treated them as the original source of Qadarite thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01394
We believe they were not the original source, although they certainly helped shape some of the ideas that later entered Qadarite doctrine when it became one of the foundations of Muʿtazilite thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01395
Take, for example, the “philosophical necessity of the human mind” discussed by Macdonald, which he treats as the source of Qadarite doctrine.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01396
In reality, this philosophical form was the higher stage to which Qadarite theory later developed.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01397

Before reaching that stage, it had remained closely connected for a long time to the realities of social and political struggle, from the killing of the third caliph, ʿUthmān, through the rise of Umayyad rule.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01398
The Umayyads gradually established a system that was almost a hereditary monarchy, with increasingly clear foundations that revealed the real character and content of the regime.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01399
This character and content were rooted in class relations.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01400
The Umayyad aristocracy gave them a religious form by adopting the doctrine of compulsion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01401
In time, this doctrine itself became one of the clearest features of Umayyad ideology, as we have already explained.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01402
The Umayyad rulers used it first as an intellectual weapon in the name of religion, and then as a weapon of violent repression against opponents from every political camp.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01403
The attempt to reconcile Qurʾānic passages, which De Boer treats as the origin of Qadarite doctrine, was in reality a result, not a cause.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01404
When social and political conditions produced the Qadarite movement, the Qadarites naturally turned to the Qurʾān in search of religious support.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01405
There they found passages that appeared to point in different directions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01406
Some could support human freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01407
Others could support divine compulsion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01408
The Qadarites therefore had to interpret passages that seemed to support compulsion in a way that brought them into harmony with passages that appeared to support human freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01409
In this way, all the passages could be read as supporting one overall meaning consistent with Qadarite doctrine.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01410
The supporters of compulsion did exactly the same thing, but in the opposite direction.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01411
That is why we say that the attempt to reconcile Qurʾānic passages was a result, not a cause.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01412
As for the influence of Christian theology, this cannot be denied.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01413
But it was an outside influence that helped internal, objective forces already at work.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01414
It also helped develop Qadarite theory and raise it toward a more philosophical level, especially once Qadarite thought entered its Muʿtazilite phase.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01414
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01415
Finally, let us look at the story told by al-Maqdisī about ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ, the first Qadarite martyr in Syria.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01416
Let us also consider the speech given by Muʿāwiya II to the people of Damascus when he decided to give up the Umayyad throne after taking the advice of his teacher, ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01417
Once again, this confirms our conclusion: Qadarite theory was connected, in both its origins and foundations, to social and political reality.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01418
When Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd asked his teacher ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ whether he should accept the inherited Umayyad caliphate, what advice did ʿAmr give him?

passage-en-01419
As we saw, he told him to accept it only if he could rule justly—and here he meant social justice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01420
Otherwise, he should step down.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01421
What does this tell us?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01422
In our view, justice was the central concern in ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ’s thinking when he had the chance to advise an Umayyad heir whom he himself had taught Qadarite doctrine.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01423
Muʿāwiya II’s speech announcing his abdication also makes it clear that his decision came from his judgment of the mistakes made by his predecessors.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01424
He believed he could not take responsibility for those mistakes or for the unjust conditions he had inherited from his grandfather Muʿāwiya I and his father Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01425
Under those inherited conditions, he did not believe he could achieve the justice demanded by the principle he had learned from his teacher, ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01426
Can we really say, then, that neither the teacher nor the student understood any connection between this “practical position” and their theoretical principle?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01427
The objective relationship between thought and action makes such a separation impossible.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01428
Thought and action are connected in the first place.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01429
And secondly, the connection exists objectively whether or not the people involved are consciously aware of it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01430
So whether ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ and his student Muʿāwiya II clearly understood this connection or not, the connection itself still existed.

passage-en-01431
And because it existed, it affected their practical behavior even if it had not entered their conscious awareness.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01432
After all this, we need to know something about the personal lives of the three major early Qadarites: Maʿbad al-Juhanī, ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

passage-en-01433
This will help us understand what these three men were really trying to achieve through Qadarite doctrine in both its theoretical and political forms.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01434
A researcher might wonder whether their preaching concealed some deeper position against Islam itself.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01435
Perhaps Qadarite doctrine was only a cover for that position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01436
Some opponents of the Qadarites at the time called their doctrine a “religious innovation” that violated the accepted foundations and principles of Islam.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01437
We saw an example of this in al-Shahrastānī’s earlier remarks, when he doubted that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī had written the letter attributed to him and addressed to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

passage-en-01438

There, al-Shahrastānī clearly treats Qadarite doctrine as something opposed to the position of the early Muslim authorities, who, in his words, believed that divine decree, “both its good and its evil,” comes from God.

passage-en-01439
So do we find anything in the lives of these three Qadarites, all of whom died while holding their doctrine, that could be used to cast doubt on their commitment to Islam?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01440
Would there be any basis for concluding that their Qadarite preaching was really aimed against Islam itself?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01441
I wanted to investigate this question in the historical sources for the period.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01442
What I found was the opposite.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01443
The historians’ accounts of all three men show not only that they were sincere Muslims, but that they were known for serious religious devotion and trusted for it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01444
I found no historian of Islamic sects—not al-Shahrastānī, al-Baghdādī or al-Isfarāyīnī—who attacked the personal religious commitment of any of the three.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01445
As for Maʿbad al-Juhanī, al-Isfarāyīnī speaks of him in a way that shows he was a transmitter of sayings from the Prophet.

passage-en-01446
That alone gave him a respected religious standing and makes it difficult to accuse him of hostility toward Islam.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01447
It was even said that Ibn Mājah, one of the well-known transmitters of hadith, narrated some reports from him.

passage-en-01448

If Maʿbad had not possessed this kind of Islamic religious standing, he could hardly have exercised the wide influence we have already described in major centers of Islamic learning such as Basra, Medina and Syria.
